html:
The Hohokam culture flourished in the Sonoran Desert of south central Arizona and northern Sonora from about 300 to about 1450, with roots that may go back to 300 BCE. Its heart was the valley of the Salt and Gila rivers, where Phoenix now stands. The map shows its area in 1492, just after it had faded.

The Hohokam dug the largest irrigation canals in North America before modern times, hundreds of kilometres of them, and grew maize, beans, squash and cotton in the desert. Large villages such as Snaketown had ball courts, which point to links with Mesoamerica, and later towns built platform mounds and big houses such as Casa Grande. They traded shell from the Gulf of California and made fine red on buff pottery.

Between about 1350 and 1450 the towns emptied, perhaps because of floods, drought and conflict. The Akimel O'odham and Tohono O'odham of the same lands count the Hohokam among their ancestors. Contemporaries farther north were the Ancestral Puebloans and the Mogollon.
